question: Following the arrival of tens of thousands of people in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on 30 July 2026, Italy reintroduced controls at air and sea borders with Spain until 16 September, in breach of the Schengen Agreement. This was a disproportionate measure considering that the Commission had declared that there were no movements of persons from Ceuta to Spain or other continental European Member States.

Spain responded by introducing controls on arrivals from Italy. Other Member States have announced plans to send back to Italy any migrants whose asylum applications should have been handled there under the Dublin system.

The action of the Italian Government risks turning a humanitarian emergency into a clash between Member States, fragmenting the Schengen area and fueling the narrative of the sovereignist far-right that the EU is incapable of acting collectively, while relegating human rights and European solidarity to the margins of political debate. We ask the Commission: 1.
Will it ask Italy to lift its border controls?
What measures will it take to ensure solidarity between Member States, a solidarity Italy has always demanded from the EU during episodes of large-scale immigration?
What measures should be taken to ensure that humanitarianism and the protection of the rights of migrants and refugees remain central to the EU’s response?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) The temporary reintroduction of internal border controls is a prerogative of the Member States. It is a measure of last resort, it must respect the principles of necessity and proportionality, and it may be applied under the conditions and limits set out in the Schengen Borders Code1.

The Commission consulted Italy and Spain on the internal border controls, and notes that they ended on 23 October 2026 and on 22 October 2026, respectively. Both the Schengen acquis and the new legislative framework of the Pact on Migration and Asylum2 are based on responsibility, solidarity and mutual trust between Member States.

The EU financial support in the field of borders management, asylum and migration as well as operational support of Home Affairs Agencies, such as the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), are also expressions of solidarity with Member States.

Furthermore, on 6 November 2026, the Commission launched the second Annual Migration Management Cycle3, according to which Greece, Spain, Cyprus and Italy are under migratory pressure, they will be eligible to access the Solidarity Pool, subject to the continued application of the responsibility rules.

Any measures in the area of border management, asylum and migration must be implemented in compliance with applicable EU and international law, including fundamental rights as guaranteed under the EU Charter.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/399 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on a Union Code
